title: Ten Sikh Gurus: Nanak to Gobind Singh
summary: Ten Sikh gurus explained for IB World Religions SL, covering key teachings, historical development, sacred texts, themes, and exam-ready comparisons.
body_markdown:
The **ten Sikh gurus** are not understood as ten isolated leaders with separate messages. In Sikh thought, they represent a continuous Guruship through which one spiritual light guided an expanding community from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh. During this period, teachings became scripture, equality became communal practice, and the Sikh community, or *Panth* , developed institutions capable of surviving persecution.


For IB World Religions SL, ask not only what each Guru did, but how each expressed and developed a shared vision. This turns a list of names into an argument about continuity, authority and adaptation. Begin with RevisionDojo’s[introduction to Sikhism](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-14-sikhism-an-introduction) , then use this guide alongside[Guru Nanak, the Ten Gurus and the Panth](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-141-sikhism-in-context-guru-nanak-the-ten-gurus-and-the-panth) .


### The ten Gurus at a glance


*Guru* means spiritual teacher or guide. In Sikhi, a respectful name many Sikhs use for their tradition, the Guru directs people away from self-centred existence and towards awareness of the divine.


Guru Development to remember


Guru Nanak Taught devotion to one divine reality, truthful living, service and rejection of social hierarchy


Guru Angad Promoted Gurmukhi literacy and strengthened the emerging community


Guru Amar Das Expanded *langar* , leadership networks and practices supporting equality


Guru Ram Das Established Ramdaspur, later Amritsar, and composed the *Lavan* hymns


Guru Arjan Compiled the Adi Granth, developed Harmandir Sahib and became the first Sikh Guru martyred


Guru Hargobind Expressed spiritual and temporal responsibility through *miri-piri*


Guru Har Rai Maintained communal strength while emphasising compassion and care


Guru Har Krishan Is remembered for service to sick and vulnerable people


Guru Tegh Bahadur Was executed after defending freedom of religious conscience


Guru Gobind Singh Founded the Khalsa and ended the mainstream line of human Gurus


Strong answers connect the rows. Guru Angad’s promotion of Gurmukhi helped preserve teachings that Guru Arjan later compiled. Guru Arjan’s martyrdom shaped the context in which Guru Hargobind articulated *miri-piri* . Sikh history accumulates rather than restarting with every Guru.


### Guru Nanak and the foundations of Sikhi


Guru Nanak lived from 1469 to 1539 in Punjab, a region shaped by encounters among Hindu, Islamic, devotional and Sufi traditions. His teaching was distinctive, not simply a mixture of neighbouring religions.


The *Mul Mantar* , which opens the Guru Granth Sahib, begins with *Ik Oankar* , affirming that divine reality is one. It describes that reality as true, creative, without fear or hatred, timeless and beyond birth. Guru Nanak also taught *hukam* , the divine order or command within which existence unfolds.


The central human problem is *haumai* , an ego-centred sense of separateness that directs attention towards status, possession and self-importance. The contrasting orientation is that of the *gurmukh* , a person directed towards the Guru, rather than the *manmukh* , one governed by self-will.


Guru Nanak connected spiritual awareness with ordinary life through three widely used principles:


- *Nam japna* : remembering and meditating upon the divine Name
- *Kirat karni* : earning honestly
- *Vand chhakna* : sharing with others


Liberation does not require withdrawal from society. A householder can seek *mukti* , liberation from ego and rebirth, through remembrance, truthful conduct and *seva* , or selfless service. RevisionDojo’s[flashcards on haumai, maya and Nam](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-712-from-manmukh-to-gurmukh-haumai-maya-and-nam/flashcards) help distinguish these connected concepts.


### From teaching community to enduring Panth


Two students reconsider whether memorising dates is enough for understanding religious history


The second through fifth Gurus transformed Guru Nanak’s community into a durable *Panth* , meaning both a religious path and the community following it.


### Guru Angad, Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das


Guru Angad promoted the Gurmukhi script, supported education and gathered Guru Nanak’s compositions. Its use gave the community an accessible means of preserving and transmitting teaching.


Guru Amar Das strengthened *langar* , the communal kitchen where people sit and eat together. Langar makes equality physical rather than merely theoretical by challenging caste hierarchy. He also developed the *manji* system of regional leadership, including women in positions of responsibility.


Guru Ram Das established Ramdaspur, which developed into Amritsar. His four *Lavan* compositions became central to the Sikh marriage ceremony, *Anand Karaj* . Together, these Gurus expressed religious authority through literacy, food, leadership, place and family life.


### Guru Arjan and sacred-text authority


Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604. It included compositions of Sikh Gurus alongside hymns associated with non-Sikh *bhagats* , including Kabir, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid. Their inclusion supports an understanding of spiritual insight that is not restricted by caste or inherited religious identity.


Guru Arjan also oversaw the completion of Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar. His execution under Mughal authority in 1606 is remembered as the first martyrdom of a Sikh Guru. It intensified the question of how a spiritual community should respond to coercion. Students can study scripture and authority together through RevisionDojo’s[Sikhism revision notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-7-sikhism/notes) .


### Miri-piri, service and religious freedom


Guru Hargobind responded to a changed political environment through *miri-piri* . *Piri* signifies spiritual authority, while *miri* signifies temporal responsibility. Tradition connects these dimensions with the Guru’s two swords and the establishment of the Akal Takht opposite Harmandir Sahib.


The concept can support legitimate defence when people face oppression, but it should not be reduced to military power. It places worldly action under ethical and spiritual discipline. Violence is not made the first choice.


Guru Har Rai maintained the community’s defensive capacity while being remembered for compassion and care. Guru Har Krishan, who became Guru as a child, is remembered for serving people during an epidemic in Delhi. Preparedness and service therefore existed together.


Guru Tegh Bahadur was executed in Delhi in 1675. Sikh tradition remembers his death as a defence of Kashmiri Pandits facing religious persecution and, more broadly, of freedom of conscience. His martyrdom connects directly with[ethics and moral conduct in Sikhism](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-76-ethics-and-moral-conduct-in-sikhism) : moral courage includes defending another community’s right to believe differently.


### Guru Gobind Singh and continuing Guruship


In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh founded the *Khalsa* , the community of initiated Sikhs committed to disciplined spiritual and ethical life. *Amrit Sanchar* and the Five Ks gave embodied form to collective identity. The names Singh and Kaur challenged inherited status, while the *sant-sipahi* , or saint-soldier, ideal joined devotion with courageous action.


Before his death in 1708, Guru Gobind Singh ended the mainstream succession of human Gurus. Guruship was vested in the **Guru Granth Sahib** , while communal authority is also associated with the **Guru Panth** . This was not merely a transfer from person to book. *Shabad Guru* means that the divine Word is Guru, encountered through recitation, singing, interpretation and lived obedience.


The Guru Granth Sahib contains *Gurbani* , the Guru’s utterance, and its pages are respectfully called *angs* , or limbs. Guru Arjan’s compilation contained compositions of the first five Gurus and other contributors. The received Guru Granth Sahib also includes hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur, while Sikh tradition associates Guru Gobind Singh with its final form.


Most mainstream Sikhs recognise the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru. Namdhari Sikhs believe that living human Guruship continued after Guru Gobind Singh. Such diversity should be presented carefully without obscuring the shared historical importance of the first ten Gurus.


### Linking the Gurus to the IB framework


The three fundamental questions organise this history into an argument:


- **What is the human condition?** People can recognise the divine, but *haumai* , attachment and self-will distort awareness.
- **Where are we going?** The goal is *mukti* , liberation from ego-driven separation and closeness to the divine.
- **How do we get there?** Through *Nam* , truthful living, honest work, sharing, worship, seva and participation in the *sangat* , or congregation.


The five themes provide another lens:


- **Doctrines and beliefs:** Ik Oankar, hukam, haumai, karma, rebirth and mukti
- **Sacred texts:** the Guru Granth Sahib as revealed Word and living Guru
- **Rituals:** Amrit Sanchar, Anand Karaj, kirtan and langar
- **Religious experience:** remembrance of Nam, congregational singing and orientation towards the Guru
- **Ethics and moral conduct:** equality, service, justice and defence of vulnerable people


For textual evidence, compare the *Mul Mantar* and discussion of hukam on Ang 1 with the teaching on Ang 62 that truthful living stands higher than abstract truth alone. Distinguish the Guru Granth Sahib from later texts such as the *Dasam Granth* , whose compilation and attribution receive different interpretations.


### How to revise the ten Sikh gurus


Do not revise ten biographies independently. Build chains such as **teaching to institution to consequence** . Guru Nanak taught equality, later Gurus embodied it through langar, and the Khalsa gave it disciplined communal form. Guru Nanak expressed revelation in hymns, Guru Angad strengthened the script, Guru Arjan compiled scripture, and Guru Gobind Singh affirmed scriptural Guruship.


Use RevisionDojo as the ultimate IB resource by combining[Sikhism key-concept flashcards](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-71-key-concepts-of-sikhism/flashcards) with Study Notes and the Questionbank. AI Chat can test comparisons, while Grading tools identify answers that list facts without explaining significance. Predicted Papers and Mock Exams develop timed judgment, while the Coursework Library and Tutors support source evaluation. The guide to[IB World Religions misconceptions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-misconceptions) also helps students avoid treating religions as internally uniform.


The deepest pattern is continuity through change. The Gurus responded differently because their circumstances differed, yet repeatedly returned to remembrance, truthful living, equality, service and justice. Once that pattern becomes visible, the names become a developing answer to what faithful life requires.
